catalog_quote: 2.5. Besides the vowel and consonant phonemes, the Picurls language has three phonemes of stress: primary / ' /, secondary /"/, and weak / w/, which will generally be left unmarked. Stress refers to the prominence of a syllable. In Picurls, stress refers to the loudness and length of the vowel nucleus, or, in some cases where the stressed syllable ends in /I m n/, the final consonant, rather than the vowel nucleus, evidences lengthening. ... Important to the structure of this language are the numerous stress sequences. Thus, /plwene/ 'rabbit' contrasts in pattern with /piwSn^/ 'rabbits'. In this example and many like it, it is the stress patterns ... that are the important marks of contrast. The stress system, therefore, is one of contrasting word superfixes, with the three levels of stress occurring in different sequences ... [p.43] word superfixes consisting of a stress pattern with …
readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so no direct conflict with it can be stated. Among the witnesses already held by the project there is a real disagreement in type: Zaharlick 1977 (following F. H. Trager 1968/1971) §2.5, p.31-32, gives Picurís 'three phonemes of stress: primary, secondary [medial], and weak' alongside three tones, states that '/píwene/ "rabbit" contrasts in pattern with /pìwénę̀/ "rabbits"' and that 'the stress system, therefore, is one of contrasting word superfixes, with the three levels of stress occurring in different sequences', and on p.48 concludes that stress placement is 'morphemic rather than phonological' (i.e. lexical, no positional rule). Sutton 2014 §6.5.1.3, p.420, says 'the status and details of tone in Picuris Tiwa are uncertain. The only available published analysis is formulated under the same rubric as George Trager's description of Taos Tiwa, a system I find highly suspect', expects instead a three-tone system like Taos (Hull 1973), and on p.421 says Nichols 1994's stress-based account of noun-suffix allomorphy is 'more likely.. based on tone'. So the Trager/Zaharlick tradition treats Picurís as having contrastive lexical stress plus tone, while Sutton treats the prominence contrasts as tone and doubts that stress is a separate contrastive category.

sources.quote: No independent Picuris stress analysis; treats the Trager/Zaharlick three-stress-three-tone system as suspect, suggests a Hull-type three-tone (high/low/falling) system with stress independent, reinterprets some 'medial stress' markings on noun suffixes as high tone, and generalises that KT lexical stress tends to be stem-initial; explicitly calls all of this speculative pending work with recordings/speakers.
sources.locator: pp.160-161 (Trager's Taos suprasegmental analysis 'strange.. suggesting it is actually erroneous', passed on to Picuris work); pp.170-171 (Zaharlick 1977 = best description; 'follows Trager's.. odd analysis of suprasegmentals'); p.408 sec 6.4.1.3; p.420 sec 6.5.1.3 'The status and details of tone in Picuris Tiwa are uncertain'; p.423 (suffixes -mǫ, -nę 'marked as medial stress high tone.. suggesting they tend to bear high tone'); p.1028 'lexical stress in Kiowa-Tanoan has a tendency to fall on the first syllable of a lexical stem'
